To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
downgrade security is a desirable property of key-exchange and that it can be achieved in practice.

(i) downgrade security is a desirable security property that should be achieved by design, (ii) the conditions for achieving downgrade security are well-known and can be applied to existing protocols, (iii) downgrade security is related to several other properties, and (iv) the design of new protocols should consider the patterns that guarantee downgrade resilience.

(a) downgrade resilience is a desirable property of key-exchange protocol designs, (b) downgrade security can be defined in terms of a set of conditions that are sufficient for it to be achieved, and (c) the conditions can be used as guidelines for the design and analysis of new protocols, and as criteria to evaluate existing ones.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of downgrade-resilient protocols, and the analysis of existing protocols to determine whether they are downgrade-resilient.
the design of key-exchange protocol modes resilient to downgrade attacks.
understanding and preventing downgrade attacks, which are a recurrent problem of configurable protocols.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, while it is possible to design downgrade-resilient protocols, it is not easy.
, for most protocols, the current state-of-practice is not good enough.
downgrade resilience is a hard property to guarantee, even for protocols that are designed from scratch with it in mind.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
downgrade resilience can be achieved with little overhead, and that it is possible to design key-exchange protocols that are secure against downgrade attacks, regardless of their configurability.
downgrade security is not a property of a single mode, but a property of a protocol, and that the security of the protocol is determined by the set of modes it supports.
downgrade resilience can be achieved by design, and is not a property that needs to be traded off against other desirable properties.
The main takeaway from our work is that

downgrade resilience is a fundamental property of key-exchange protocol, and that its analysis requires the use of tools and techniques that are orthogonal to the ones used to study other security properties.
, while it is hard to achieve downgrade security for all modes of a protocol, it is possible to do so for a large subset.
